name: Hints, Not Answers
title: Hints, Not Answers
answer: Hints, not answers means configuring a general AI tool so it guides a student through a math problem instead of solving it for them. The idea matters because a plain chatbot can lift practice performance while leaving students worse on a later exam taken without AI, while a hint-based tutor avoided that loss in the cited trial. The school's job is to set the tool's standing instructions and prepare the hints it may use.

sections.body: Most general AI tools will solve a math problem as soon as a student asks, which makes them poor tutors even when they seem helpful. The problem is that a student can get correct practice answers without doing the reasoning, and the cited high school trial found that this pattern came with a later exam cost. To turn the same kind of tool into a tutor, a school sets standing instructions that shape how it responds. The tool should ask what the student has tried, offer one hint at a time, and never show a full solution. This idea solves the gap between a tool that produces answers and a tool that supports learning.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In mathematics across kindergarten through twelfth grade, the teacher's setup decides whether the tool acts as a tutor or an answer machine. With a school account in a tool such as Gemini for Education, a teacher can give standing instructions to ask what the student has tried, give one hint at a time, and never show a full solution. Figure 7.3 lists the instructions that matter most. The best setups also give the tool the correct answer, and in the high school trial the tutor version received each problem's solution so it would not invent a wrong one while guiding the student. Teachers also add common mistakes with a matching hint for each, which takes time but can be reused every year the unit is taught.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this as the strongest evidence in the chapter and presents it as a warning. In a high school math trial, students using a plain chatbot during practice scored much higher on practice problems but 17 percent lower on a later exam taken without AI (Bastani et al., 2025). Students using a tutor set up to give hints rather than answers did not suffer that loss. The difference came down to how the tool was configured.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The main risk is that a general AI tool will solve the problem the moment a student asks, which can produce strong practice scores and weaker later performance without AI. The cited trial shows that a plain chatbot was linked to a 17 percent lower exam score, so the configuration is not a minor detail. The decisions stay with the teacher and school: what standing instructions to use, what correct answer to supply, and which common mistakes and matching hints to add. The tool must be set up so it does not invent a wrong solution while guiding the student. Preparation takes time, and that work remains a human responsibility even when the hints can be reused each year the unit is taught.
